<reason>Both sides fought a genuinely clean, narrowing debate, but A built the more decisive route. B's two best lines — the "such as" scope argument and the gut-feel counterfactual — were both directly addressed: A gave a clear, principled scope answer (the motion's stated reason, "too little predictive validity," identifies which members of the category are targeted), which reduced B's scope play to something A could fairly label wordplay; and A's "bias with a score attached / cheap structure is free" reply kept the counterfactual contested rather than conceded. Meanwhile A extracted and exploited B's central concession under pressure: B's answer to Q1 was "keep using them... with the letter as a headline you can ignore." A's closing turned that into a memorable, substantive point — the products employers actually buy, name workshops after, and print on mugs and email signatures are the letters, so B was defending a different instrument inside the same packaging, and DISC was "borrowing credibility from a measure it isn't." B's rejoinder (the motion's verb is abolition, not headline reform) is real and kept B alive, but it left B defending continuous scales whose worth B could only assert, while A's harms weighing (a durable, logoed, flippable label carried into staffing and promotion versus a conversation two colleagues could have had unaided) went only partly answered — B's "the four-minute chat causes the harm" does not rebut the marginal harm the label adds. B did land two real hits: A conceded workshops need no prediction bar, which strains the motion's stated reason on the team-building half, and A's own "tests sit on top of the chat" line was neatly turned. Both sides used A1:/A2: labels properly, but B's two clipped over-length rebuttals are an execution cost, cutting off the end of the counterfactual push.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's exploitation of B's Pressure-Question answer — "keep using them, read the letter as a headline you can ignore" — recast as a concession: nobody buys DISC for the intensity graph, the workshop is named after the letters, so B abandoned the part actually in use. B's "the motion's verb is abolition, not headline reform" was the best available reply but could not undo the concession's rhetorical and substantive damage.</best_rebuttal>
